title: Engagement as Attitude: A Bifactor Measure of Employee Engagement
text: Full title: Engagement as attitude: Development and initial validation of an intentional bi-factor measure of employee engagement Authors: John Kulas, Renata Garcia Prieto Palacios Roji, Casey Osorio-Duffoo, Morgan Russell, & Mike DeFabiis Code: jtkulas/EngagementPaper

title: Engagement as Attitude: A Bifactor Measure of Employee Engagement
text:
About the paper
Engagement is usually defined by three sub-dimensions: vigor, dedication, and absorption. Attitudes are usually split into cognitive, affective, and behavioral components. This paper develops and validates an 18-item measure that intentionally crosses both models, so every item captures one dimension from each.

title: Engagement as Attitude: A Bifactor Measure of Employee Engagement
text:
Data & methods

Snowball sample: 282 working adults, with items shown in four counterbalanced orders
Qualtrics panel: 343 adults saw items grouped by attitude; 404 saw items grouped by substantive dimension
Reliabilities ranged from α = 0.78 to 0.91 across the six subscales
Confirmatory factor analyses across 1,025 respondents showed fair fit for both the substantive and attitudinal structures (RMSEA = 0.09)

title: Engagement as Attitude: A Bifactor Measure of Employee Engagement
text:
Key findings

Grouping items by dimension gave respondents only slight cues about the structure; the item-order effect was small
Measurement invariance held across the four snowball-sample conditions, but not across all six conditions once the panel samples were added
The main source of misfit was the scale’s single reverse-coded item (“Thinking about work saps my energy”)

title: Engagement as Attitude: A Bifactor Measure of Employee Engagement
text:
My contributions

Automated cleaning of messy free-text survey responses (for example, “hours worked”) so the code works on new data as it arrives
Recoded reverse-scored items, split and merged data across survey conditions, and ran item analysis
Built interactive plots of results
Ran the confirmatory factor analyses and fit the bifactor model, including troubleshooting models that wouldn’t converge
In 2023, cleaned up the code base, documented each data source, and got the APA-formatted manuscript knitting to PDF

title: Bifactor Engagement Measure: SIOP 2022 & 2023 Posters
text: Conferences: Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology (SIOP) Annual Conference, Seattle 2022 & Boston 2023 Collaborators: John Kulas, Morgan Russell, Renata Garcia Prieto Palacios Roji, Mike DeFabiis Code: heyimMIKE123/Engagement-Survey-Projects · Technical report

title: Bifactor Engagement Measure: SIOP 2022 & 2023 Posters
text:
The idea
Researchers usually describe engagement in one of two ways: by substance (Vigor, Dedication, Absorption) or by attitude (what you Think, Feel, and Do). Instead of picking one, our team wrote items that measure both at once. Each item maps to one substantive and one attitudinal dimension, which gives broad coverage of the construct with a short survey.

title: Bifactor Engagement Measure: SIOP 2022 & 2023 Posters
text:
SIOP 2023: Construct and criterion-related validation


Gave the scale to a Qualtrics panel alongside two established engagement measures (UWES and Saks), an intent-to-quit scale, and two unrelated “discriminant” scales (pets, household activities)
Screened out careless responders (excessive missing data, straight-lining, speeding), keeping 377 of 743 respondents
Found strong convergent validity (r = .79 with Saks, .81 with UWES) and a meaningful negative link to intent to quit (r = −.39)

Download the 2023 poster (PDF)

title: Bifactor Engagement Measure: SIOP 2022 & 2023 Posters
text:
SIOP 2022: Developing the measure


Wrote 50 items, then kept the 36 that graduate students and faculty sorted most consistently
Collected responses from 330 working adults through snowball sampling
Reduced to 20 items using two parallel methods: corrected item-total correlations and CFA modification indices
The bifactor model fit well: CFI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.07; subscale alphas ranged from 0.69 to 0.86

Read the full report (PDF)

title: 2021 State of Culture Report
text:
The question
During the COVID-19 pandemic, some organizations adapted and even innovated while others struggled. What aspects of organizational culture separated the two?

title: 2021 State of Culture Report
text:
The study

Survey: a 70-item survey covering culture, climate, performance, COVID-19 responses, values, and social justice practices (Likert-scale and open-ended items)
Sample: 241 respondents from more than 200 organizations across six continents, including HR/OD and non-HR professionals and roles from individual contributor to executive
Collection: six weeks of snowball sampling through professional networks and social media
Framework: gothamCulture’s Culture Mosaic, which scores four culture dimensions: Inspire, Deliver, Enable, and Adapt

title: 2021 State of Culture Report
text:
Key findings










Culture predicted adaptability. Organizations that pivoted or innovated during the pandemic scored significantly higher on all four Culture Mosaic dimensions, for example Enable (79 vs. 61) and Adapt (78 vs. 53).
Defining culture matters. Organizations with a shared definition of culture, especially one shaped by leadership, scored significantly higher on all four dimensions. Only 44% had one.
Measurement isn’t action. Only 36% formally measured culture, and just 21% said their assessments led to real change, a clear gap between data and action.
Remote work is here to stay. 68% expected remote work to continue after the pandemic.
Social justice: organizations that discussed social justice openly and honestly significantly outperformed those that treated it as “lip service.”

title: Bought but Partially Sold? Measurement Invariance Across Purchased and Snowball Samples
text: Authors: John Kulas, Casey Osorio-Duffoo, Mike DeFabiis, & Morgan Russell Role: Second author Code: jtkulas/EngagementPaper · Engagement-Survey-Projects

title: Bought but Partially Sold? Measurement Invariance Across Purchased and Snowball Samples
text:
The question
Over the past 15 years, organizations and researchers have increasingly bought survey responses from online panels such as Qualtrics and Prolific instead of recruiting volunteers. These panels are fast, but data quality questions remain. Do people from purchased panels interpret a survey the same way as people who volunteered to take it?

title: Bought but Partially Sold? Measurement Invariance Across Purchased and Snowball Samples
text:
Approach
We tested the measurement invariance of our 18-item engagement survey (see the engagement paper) across samples, first three and then five:

Voluntary snowball sample (n = 232)
Qualtrics panel, cleaned (from 743 respondents)
Prolific panel, cleaned (from 785 respondents)
Qualtrics respondents flagged as careless
Prolific respondents flagged as careless










Using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in lavaan, we compared configural, metric, and scalar models to see where the samples’ responses diverged.

title: Bought but Partially Sold? Measurement Invariance Across Purchased and Snowball Samples
text:
My contributions

Combined all three survey sources into one cleaned analysis data set, with documented sample sources and response dates
Wrote and maintained the measurement invariance analysis in R Markdown
